[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]

[[Category: Adams County, Ohio]]

== Biography ==
Robert was born in 1804. He was the son of [[Glasgow-563|William Glasgow]] and [[Montgomery-6593|Rhoda Montgomery]].  He passed away in 1882.
== Research Notes ==
=== Individual father review, 22 October 2026 ===

The existing father [[Glasgow-563]] is assessed at 73% (probable). The specific inherited family account calls Robert Barclay the son of William and Rhoda Montgomery. His 1804 generation fits William’s established family, and the name repeats the known earlier Robert Barclay family. The held citation is only a memorial and no named-parent original is available.

Probable73%; the family attribution and naming are dependent clues, not independently inspected proofs.

Next useful test: Check Faris’s William/Rhoda children and the memorial’s actual underlying evidence.

Source basis already held: [https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-835 WikiTree profile export for Glasgow-835]. No new original inspected; no new father attached.

=== Faris family Bible account, 24 October 2026 ===

David Faris’s ''The Glasgow Family of Adams County, Ohio'' (1990), pp. 32–33 and 46–47, identifies Robert Barclay Glasgow (born 26 November 1804) as a son of William and Rhoda. It gives his marriages to Phoebe McFall and Matilda Jane Campbell and traces his move from Ohio to Washington County, Iowa, matching the existing spouse profiles and vital dates. Faris says the exact names and birth dates came from William and Rhoda’s family Bible, held by Mrs E. R. Harvey of Washington, Iowa, on 25 June 1927. The book also transmits a 14 May 1928 letter by descendant Grace G. Glasgow, who recalls “Uncle Robert,” uncle Madison and grandfather Joseph on adjoining Ohio farms, including the old homestead where William lived.

This evidence supports the existing [[Glasgow-835|Robert Barclay Glasgow]] → [[Glasgow-563|William Glasgow]] father relationship at 94% confident inference, from 73% probable. Faris provides a specific family account and descendant recollection, not direct biological proof; the Bible and originals underlying census accounts remain uninspected. Its maternal surname/date inconsistencies do not justify changing a mother, vital date, or other relationship. Next test: locate the original family Bible or its probate/custody trail.
